name: Wallis and Futuna
summary_text: Wallis and Futuna is a territorial collectivity of the French Republic and stands under the French national framework: the civil and criminal codes of France apply locally unless a local measure overrides them. No law in force criminalises trans people or same-sex relations, and discrimination on grounds of gender identity has been prohibited since the 2012 statutory extension covering employment, housing and access to services.  Legal gender-marker change is available on the basis of the 2016-17 French reforms, which removed the requirement for surgery or a psychiatric diagnosis. A trans visitor whose documents already reflect their lived gender can present them without entering a separate local procedure. French law recognises no non-binary status, so a third-gender or X marker cannot be obtained.  Nothing in the sources indicates trans-specific screening at entry or in local administrative processing. Practical exposure to harm is concentrated in two areas: detention and everyday social conditions. Under the French prison framework that applies here, trans women whose legal gender is marked male, largely those without reassignment surgery, are held in all-male establishments, a situation described in reporting as a documented legal grey area; one such transfer to a men's facility in Lille took place in 2014.

sources.documents: Institutional human-rights report documenting significant issues with gender-affirming healthcare provision in France: lack of self-determination, extended waiting times, inequitable access by location; recommends informed consent model.

sources.title: Law banning conversion therapy - Senate 7 Dec 2020, National Assembly 25 Jan 2022, published 1 Feb 2022
sources.documents: Legally bans conversion therapy with punishments of two years imprisonment and/or 30,000 euro fine; documents state protection against forced conversion practices.

name: Samoa
summary_text: Samoa's Crimes Act 2013 criminalises same-sex sexual activity, with penalties of up to five years' imprisonment, as recorded in the Human Dignity Trust country profile. The offence is framed by the sexual act rather than by the partners' identity, so it applies equally where one partner is transgender. A trans visitor in a same-sex relationship should treat Samoa as a jurisdiction where that conduct is a criminal offence carrying a custodial penalty.  The same statute removed the colonial-era offence of impersonating a woman, so no Samoan law targets gender expression itself. RNZ Pacific reported on 3 May 2013 that the new Crimes Act was in force that week and that Samoa Fa'afafine Association president To'oto'oali'i Roger Stanley expressed relief at the repeal. The same reporting records that the community was not at that time agitating for repeal of the sodomy provisions, so the decriminalisation position on that front remained unchanged.  Gender-diverse identity is culturally embedded in Samoa. The Samoa Fa'afafine Association's stakeholder report for Samoa's Universal Periodic Review at the 39th session in 2021, titled 'The Protection of the Rights of Fa'afafine/Fa'atama/LGBTIQ/SOGIESC persons in Samoa', describes the third-gender identities fa'afafine and fa'atama and documents lived experiences and struggles, with the stated aim of establishing grounds for non-discriminatory policy and legislation. That report is an advocacy submission rather than a source of binding protection, and the inventory does not establish any statutory mechanism for changing gender markers.

sources.title: Crimes Act 2013 (Tulafono o Solitulafono 2013), Sections 67, 68, 71
sources.documents: Current criminalization of sodomy, attempts to commit sodomy, and keeping place of resort for homosexual acts; punishable by up to 5-7 years imprisonment; also prohibits heterosexual anal intercourse and oral sex.
sources.detail: Cited as Sections 67, 68, and 71; Act took effect on 1 May 2013; no URL visible in text
